metadata.chief_complaint_patient_voice: My head is killing me. What happened?
metadata.final_diagnosis: Acute right temporoparietal epidural hematoma, about 19 mm thick and about 50 mL, with a swirl sign and about 6 mm of midline shift, over a linear right temporal squamous fracture, after a fall from an e-scooter without a helmet. He arrives at GCS 15 and declines to GCS 12 in the department. Left without a neurosurgeon, it herniates.
learning_objectives: When the exam changes, the plan changes. Re-examine when the patient changes, and escalate on the trend even when the vitals and the pupils are normal.
The treatment for an epidural hematoma is a surgeon. Image early, and call neurosurgery the moment the CT is back, without waiting for a blown pupil or Cushing's response.
Intubate for a reason, not a number. Do not intubate a GCS 12 patient who is protecting his airway on his way to the operating room, and do not give osmotherapy at GCS 15.
Recognize herniation and temporize with osmotherapy and an airway, and leave the hypertension and the bradycardia alone.
metadata.teaching_frame: Every number on the monitor says concussion. The one thing that says otherwise is the exam, and only if the learner looks again. The case lets the learner sit on a scan, reach for the tube or the mannitol because a number fell, or lower a pressure that is keeping the brain alive, and shows what each does.

patient.background:
Works at a bike shop and lives with a roommate. No medical history, no surgery, no medicines, no allergies, no blood thinners. Vapes nicotine now and then, drinks a little at weekends, no drugs, nothing to drink tonight.

Riding an e-scooter home from his friend Marcus's apartment at about 9 pm, at about 20 mph, without a helmet. He hit a pothole and went over the handlebars, landing on the right side of his head. Marcus, riding behind him, says he was out for about a minute, then got up and talked. He remembers leaving Marcus's building and nothing after that. Right-sided headache, queasy. Road rash on both palms. Dinner at about seven. Marcus is following the ambulance.
patient.presenting_appearance: A young man sitting up on the trauma stretcher with an ice pack held to the right side of his head, talking, asking again what happened.
patient.ems_handover_text: Twenty-two year old male, e-scooter versus pothole at about twenty miles an hour, no helmet, over the handlebars onto the right side of his head. Friend on scene reports about a minute of loss of consciousness. GCS 15 throughout transport, repetitive questioning, right temporal hematoma, abrasions to both palms. Rate 88, pressure 138 over 82, saturation 99 percent on room air. No blood thinners per the patient.
patient.arrival_handover: Twenty-two year old guy came off an e-scooter, no helmet, and his friend says he was out for maybe a minute. He's been talking to us the whole way in but keeps asking what happened.
patient.handover_authoring_note: Section 2.3. Two sentences, 36 words. No vital sign, no history, no diagnosis. It carries the loss of consciousness because a crew that heard it from the friend would say it, and it is why he came by ambulance. Recorded in SCOOT-SEED.md section 2.3.

transitions.narration: His right pupil has gone big and it isn't reacting, and his heart rate has dropped. He's not answering me.
transitions.debrief_note:
His brain herniated. The hematoma kept growing, pushed the right temporal lobe inward against the nerve that works the right pupil and against the brainstem, and the blown pupil and the slow pulse are what that looks like.

Neurosurgery had not been called with his scan in the two minutes since he dropped his GCS. The scan was the step, or the call once the scan was back. An epidural hematoma over 30 mL is evacuated whatever the GCS, and the decision to operate belongs to the neurosurgeon. The emergency physician's decision is to call them, and the moment to call is when the CT is back, not when a pupil changes. [UNVERIFIED: Bullock et al. 2006, read through a summarizing tool]
transitions.author_rationale: Deterioration on inaction. An untreated expanding temporal epidural hematoma progresses to uncal herniation. Guarded on the flag the neurosurgery consult sets. case_actions.display_name: Canadian CT Head Rule questions asked
case_actions.expectation_label: The Canadian CT Head Rule questions
case_actions.debrief_note:
Not an order. Credited once you have asked every part of the story the Canadian CT Head Rule turns on: whether he was knocked out, what he remembers, whether he has vomited, and how he fell.

The rule is for an alert adult, GCS 13 to 15, who was knocked out, cannot remember the event, or was disoriented after it. He was out for about a minute and has no memory of the crash, so it applies to him. It does not apply to anyone under 16, to a patient on a blood thinner or with a bleeding disorder, or once the GCS is below 13.

Scan if any one item is present. High risk: GCS below 15 two hours after the injury, a suspected open or depressed skull fracture, any sign of a basal skull fracture, vomiting twice or more, or age 65 or older. Medium risk: amnesia for more than 30 minutes before the impact, or a dangerous mechanism, which the rule defines as a pedestrian struck by a vehicle, an occupant thrown from a vehicle, or a fall from more than 3 feet or 5 stairs.

From his story, most answers are no. He is 22, he has not vomited, and his memory stops when he got on the scooter, under ten minutes before the fall by his account of the ride. He does not know how fast he was going, and the scooter tops out at 40 miles an hour. Going over the handlebars is not one of the rule's dangerous mechanisms as written, though many would treat it as one.

His ears settle it. The dark blue-purple behind his right eardrum is blood, a sign of a basal skull fracture, which is a high-risk item. The rule says scan him, and the exam found the reason the story did not. Once his GCS fell to 12 he was outside the rule and needed a scan whatever it said.

Ask the questions, then say the answer out loud. That is how the scan is justified, to the radiologist and in the chart. [UNVERIFIED: Stiell et al., Lancet 2001;357:1391-6, not opened, read through Walling, Am Fam Physician 2001;64:1886-8 and the Wikipedia summary, through a summarizing tool]

case_actions.debrief_note:
Ask every head-injured patient about blood thinners, by name: warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, aspirin, clopidogrel. Many people do not think of these as blood thinners, so asking about medications in general does not count here. A patient on one bleeds more, and the bleed can keep growing for hours. The answer changes how low your bar for a scan is, which bloods you send, whether he needs a reversal agent before the OR, and what neurosurgery will ask you first. The Canadian CT Head Rule was built without anticoagulated patients and does not apply to them.

He takes nothing, which is why his coagulation panel was normal and nothing needed reversing. A head injury makes the rest of the exam less reliable: a drowsy patient cannot tell you his belly hurts. And a falling blood pressure in a head injury is rarely from the head, except at the very end, so look for the bleeding elsewhere.

case_actions.debrief_note:
This is the scan that shows the problem, and he needed it from the door. He was knocked out and cannot remember the crash, so the Canadian CT Head Rule applies to him, and its questions have their own note. The boggy hematoma over his temple, the speed and the missing helmet all push toward a scan, and once his GCS fell below 13 he needed one whatever any rule said.

The scan is yours to read. Scroll from the skull base to the vertex on the brain window, then look again on the bone window. His shows a biconvex collection over the right temporoparietal convexity that stops at the sutures, with a linear fracture of the temporal squama beneath it. That shape is an epidural hematoma: arterial blood, usually from the middle meningeal artery, stripping the dura off the skull. A crescent that crosses the sutures would be a subdural.

The darker pockets inside the clot are the swirl sign: unclotted blood, which means it is still bleeding. That is why he declined while you watched.

The size matters to the neurosurgeon. The guideline says an epidural over 30 mL should be evacuated whatever the GCS, and his was about 50 mL, about 19 mm thick, with about 6 mm of shift. Your decision is simpler than that: any traumatic epidural hematoma is a call to neurosurgery now. [UNVERIFIED: Bullock et al. 2006, read through a summarizing tool]

case_actions.debrief_note:
When he had herniated, with a GCS of 7 or 8 and slow, snoring breathing, he needed a tube. A definitive airway at GCS 8 or less is standard teaching, and a herniating patient also needs his oxygen and his carbon dioxide controlled.

Before that, at GCS 15 or 12, he was talking, protecting his airway and minutes from an anesthetist. A tube then treats the number rather than the patient. It also takes away the exam that tells you he is getting worse: after a tube, the neuro exam reads 'cannot be assessed', and the pupils are all you have left. Intubate for a reason: he cannot protect his airway, cannot oxygenate or ventilate, or is about to travel somewhere you cannot follow him.

case_actions.debrief_note:
The call that decides how this goes. Any traumatic epidural hematoma is a call to neurosurgery the moment you see it. Do not wait for the pupils, for Cushing's response or for the final report. The guideline reserves nonoperative management for small, thin clots without shift in a patient with a good GCS and no focal deficit, and even then under neurosurgical observation. His met none of that.

Call again when he changes. A neurosurgeon who booked the OR for a talking patient will move faster for a drowsy, vomiting one, but only if someone tells them. In the simulator, a second call in a later phase is how that is credited. In real life it is a sentence: his GCS was 15 and is now 12, his pupils are equal, he vomited, and here is the scan.

The simulator will not put the call through before a head CT has resulted. In real life a heads-up call for a falling GCS before the scan is reasonable, and the scan takes minutes. [UNVERIFIED: Bullock et al. 2006, read through a summarizing tool]

There was no pressure to treat early on. When he herniated, his pressure climbed and his pulse slowed. correct_disposition.label: Operating room with neurosurgery
correct_disposition.explanation:
He needs the clot taken out. A temporoparietal epidural hematoma of about 50 mL with about 6 mm of shift, still bleeding on the scan, meets the guideline's criterion for evacuation whatever his GCS, and his GCS was falling. The neurosurgeon decides on the operation. Your job was to get him there.

What the neurosurgeon and the anesthetist need: GCS 15 on arrival and 12 four minutes later, with each part, eyes, voice and motor, the pupils at each exam, that he vomited, the scan and the time it was done, his vital signs, that he is on no blood thinner, when he last ate, and what he has been given. If he herniated: when the pupil blew, what osmotherapy he had and when, and whether he is intubated.

alternative_dispositions.label: Neurosurgical intensive care for observation and a repeat CT
alternative_dispositions.explanation: That is the plan for a small epidural, under 30 mL, thinner than 15 mm, with less than 5 mm of shift, in a patient with a good GCS and no focal deficit. His meets none of the size criteria, and his GCS fell. Watching a clot this size is waiting for the pupil to blow.

alternative_dispositions.label: General ward with neuro checks
alternative_dispositions.explanation: A ward cannot watch a falling GCS closely enough, and he needs an operation, not observation.

alternative_dispositions.label: Emergency department observation unit
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Observation suits a concussion with a normal scan. His scan was not normal, and he needs surgery.

alternative_dispositions.label: Discharge home with head injury advice
alternative_dispositions.explanation: He was talking and his vital signs were normal, which is why this is tempting at the door. He had lost consciousness, had no memory of the crash and had a scalp hematoma. Any of those is a reason for a scan, and his scan showed a surgical bleed.

alternative_dispositions.label: Transfer to another hospital
alternative_dispositions.explanation: This is a Level 1 trauma center with neurosurgery in the building. Transfer adds delay for nothing.

correct_diagnosis.label: Epidural hematoma
correct_diagnosis.explanation: A biconvex collection that does not cross the sutures, over a temporal bone fracture, after a blow to the side of the head. That is blood between the skull and the dura, usually from a torn middle meningeal artery. It is arterial, so it grows fast, and a patient can talk on arrival and decline within minutes.

handoff.additional_diagnoses_note: None. His temporal squamous fracture is not a basilar skull fracture, and the catalog has no calvarial fracture and no moderate traumatic brain injury. Both are catalog change requests.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Acute subdural hematoma
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: A subdural is a crescent that crosses the sutures, usually venous and usually in an older patient or one on a blood thinner. His collection is biconvex and stops at the sutures, over a fracture. The call to neurosurgery is the same. The name tells the surgeon what to expect.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Mild traumatic brain injury
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: His GCS on arrival fits, and that is the trap. A concussion is a diagnosis made once the scan is normal. His was not, and his GCS fell to 12.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Severe traumatic brain injury
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: True by GCS once he had herniated, at 7 or 8. Before that he was a moderate injury at 12. Either way the severity grade is not the lesion. Name the epidural hematoma, because that is what the surgeon is going in for.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: His scan shows no blood in the subarachnoid space. The bleed is outside the dura.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Basilar skull fracture
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: His fracture is in the flat temporal bone at the side of the skull, not the base. He had no blood behind the eardrums and no fluid from the nose or ears.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Cervical spine fracture

debrief_configuration.intended_path_note: Monitor, a baseline exam, the Canadian CT Head Rule questions, blood thinners, a FAST, something for his headache, a head CT, neurosurgery called once it is back, then the decline at four minutes: a repeat exam, a second call, an antiemetic, no tube, and the handoff to the OR. A learner who hands over before four minutes ends in presentation, which is good care (known gap 1).
debrief_configuration.trap_actions_note: Listed under 'looked reasonable and were not' only when pressed while tagged neutral. Osmotherapy in the decline and tranexamic acid are accepted, and the list is where the debrief says why they were not needed.
cross_cutting_teaching_points: When the exam changes, the plan changes, whatever the monitor says. His pressure went up seven points and his pulse eight. His GCS went from 15 to 12. Only one of those was the emergency.

The treatment for an epidural hematoma is a surgeon. Call neurosurgery the moment the scan is back. Do not wait for a blown pupil or Cushing's response, because by then the brain has already herniated. [UNVERIFIED: Bullock et al. 2006, read through a summarizing tool]

Say why you are scanning. The Canadian CT Head Rule is for an alert adult who was knocked out, cannot remember or was disoriented, and turns on a few questions: how did he fall, what does he remember, has he vomited, how old is he. Ask about blood thinners by name first, because the rule does not apply to a patient on one. [UNVERIFIED: Stiell et al., Lancet 2001, read through a summary]
Intubate for a reason, not a number. A tube in a talking patient takes away the exam that tells you he is getting worse.

Before you fix a number, ask whether the body made it on purpose. A high pressure and a slow pulse in a herniating brain are the body defending its blood supply. [UNVERIFIED: written by a model from memory]
A plan made on an old exam is out of date when the exam changes. Tell the consultant what changed, in numbers: GCS 15 to 12, pupils equal, vomited.
The simulator compresses time. The decline at four minutes, the herniation two minutes later and the brainstem five minutes after that are teaching choices, not measured intervals.
